To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the quality of the optics is determined by the quality of the mirror substrate; 2) the quality of multilayer mirror coatings can be characterized in situ and in real-time; 3) the quality of single layer mirror coatings can be determined in real-time by a combination of in situ characterization and ex situ slope metrology; and 4) the quality of mirror substrates can be characterized by a combination of ex situ slope metrologies and ex situ surface metrologies

(1) the slope accuracy of single crystal silicon mirror substrates can be improved to better than 0.1 arcsec, (2) the slope accuracy and roughness of multilayer coatings can be improved by more than an order of magnitude to below 0.1 and 0.3 arcsec and 0.2 nm respectively, and (3) the slope accuracy can be improved for very long substrates to better than 2 arcsec

the slope accuracy of 1.5 nm rms (peak to valley 3.5 nm) can be achieved with a 1 m long mirror substrate, which has a 0.1 mm rms figure error, using the current technology of single and multilayer mirror coatings, and the current state-of-the-art ex-situ slope measuring defleomter.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the characterization of ultraprecisely figured X-ray optics.
the development of novel metrology concepts and their implementation for the characterization of ultraprecisely manufactured X-ray optics.

the following aspects: (1) the design of new optical components for the next generation of synchrotrons, (2) the development of new coating techniques for these components, and (3) the development of novel metrology tools to measure the surface and coating topography of the optical components.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current state of the art of X-ray optical metrology is sufficient to characterize the quality of ultralow roughness mirrors and gratings.
, although the state-of-the-art of X-ray optics is already very advanced, there are still a lot of challenges to overcome in order to reach the ultimate limits of X-ray optics.
the present state-of-the art of the X-ray optics is not sufficient for the next generation of X-ray free electron lasers (XFEL) which require optics with a surface figure of 0.1 nm rms and better.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the quality of the optical components is limited by the quality of the substrates, and that the quality of substrates is limited by the current state-of-the-art polishing and grinding technology, which is not able to produce substrates of the quality needed for the next generation of high-precision X-ray optics.
we are now able to produce and measure very long mirrors with a slope accuracy of 0.2 arcseconds and an accuracy of the surface figure of 0.1 nm rms.

the current state of the art of X-ray optical metrology is not able to fully characterize the quality of ultrahigh-precision X-ray optical components, especially for the characterization of the surface topography.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current ex situ metrology is not sufficient to characterize the optical quality of ultra-precisely figured optics.

for a full characterization of ultraprecisely figured X-ray optics the use of slope measuring deflecontmetry is essential, but that for the characterization of the surface quality of multilayer coated optics the use of white beam interferometry is required.
the characterization and optimization of the quality of ultrasmooth optics is a very challenging task, which is still far from being fully solved.
